risks.title: Insufficient access controls
risks.description: Effective access management is fundamental to data security, ensuring only authorized individuals or groups can access specific datasets. Such security protocols encompass authentication, authorization and finely tuned access controls tailored to the scope of access required by each user, down to the file or record level. Establishing definitive governance policies for data access is imperative in response to the heightened risks from data breaches and regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). These policies guard against unauthorized use and are a cornerstone of preserving data integrity and maintaining customer trust.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to authenticate and limit who can access your data and AI platform
• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to authorize access to data
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists to limit IP addresses that can authenticate to your data and AI platform
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as a strong control that limits the source for inbound requests
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources 
• DASF 51: Share data and AI assets securely
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to track access to data, AI and other resources
• DASF 59: Use clean rooms to collaborate in a secure environment
• DASF 67: Federate authentication

risks.title: Missing data classification
risks.description: Data classification is critical for data governance, enabling organizations to effectively sort and categorize data by sensitivity, importance and criticality. As data volumes grow exponentially, prioritizing sensitive information protection, risk reduction and data quality becomes imperative. Classification facilitates the implementation of appropriate security measures and governance policies by evaluating data’s risk and value. A robust classification strategy strengthens data governance, mitigates risks, and ensures data integrity and security on a scalable level.

risks.title: Poor data quality
risks.description: Data quality is crucial for reliable data-driven decisions and is a cornerstone of data governance. Malicious actors threaten data integrity, accuracy and consistency, challenging the analytics and decision-making processes that depend on high-quality data, just as a well-intentioned user with poor-quality data can limit the efficacy of an AI system. To safeguard against these threats, organizations must rigorously evaluate key data attributes — accuracy, completeness, freshness and rule compliance. Prioritizing data quality enables organizations to trace data lineage, apply data quality rules and monitor changes, ensuring analytical accuracy and cost-effectiveness.

• DASF 7: Enforce data quality checks on batch and streaming datasets 
• DASF 21: Monitor data and AI system from a single pane of glass 
• DASF 36: Set up monitoring alerts

risks.title: Legality of data
risks.description: Intellectual property concerns of training data and and legal mandates — such as those from GDPR, CCPA and LGPD — necessitate the capability of machine learning systems to “delete” specific data. But you often can’t “untrain” a model; during the training process, input data is encoded into the internal representation of the model, characterized by elements like thresholds and weights, which could become subject to legal constraints. Tracking your training data and retraining your model using clean and ownership-verified datasets is essential for meeting regulatory demands.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 12: Delete records from datasets and retrain models to forget data subjects
• DASF 27: Pretrain a large language model (LLM) to only use the data that is allowed with LLMs for inference
• DASF 29: Build MLOps workflows to track models and trace data sources and lineage to retrain models with the updated dataset by following legal constraints

risks.title: Adversarial partitions
risks.description: If an attacker can influence the partitioning of datasets used in training and evaluation, they can effectively exercise indirect control over the ML system by making them vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where carefully crafted inputs lead to incorrect outputs. These attacks can exploit the space partitioning capabilities of machine learning models, such as tree ensembles and neural networks, leading to misclassifications even in high-confidence scenarios. This form of “model control” can lead to biased or compromised outcomes. Therefore, it is crucial that datasets accurately reflect the intended operational reality of the ML system. Implementing stringent security measures to safeguard against such manipulations is essential for maintaining the integrity and reliability of ML systems.

risks.title: Data poisoning
risks.description: Attackers can compromise an ML system by contaminating its training data to manipulate its output at the inference stage. All three initial components of a typical ML system — raw data, data preparation and datasets — are susceptible to poisoning attacks. Intentionally manipulated data, possibly coordinated across these components, derail the ML training process and create an unreliable model. Practitioners must assess the potential extent of training data an attacker might control internally and externally and the resultant risks.

risks.title: Lack of tracking and reproducibility of experiments
risks.description:
ML development is often poorly documented and tracked, and results that cannot be reproduced may lead to overconfidence in an ML system’s performance. Common issues include: 
Critical details missing from a model’s description 

Results that are fragile, producing dramatically different results on a different GPU (even one that is supposed to be spec-identical) 

Extensive tweaks to the authors’ system until it outperforms the untweaked “baseline,” resulting in asserted improvements that aren’t borne out in practice (particularly common in academic work)


Additionally, adversaries may gain initial access to a system by compromising the unique portions of the ML supply chain. This could include the model itself, training data or its annotations, parts of the ML software stack, or even GPU hardware. In some instances, the attacker will need secondary access to fully carry out an attack using compromised supply chain components.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 20: Track ML training runs for documenting, measuring, versioning and tracking model artifacts including algorithms, training environment, hyperparameters, metrics and results
• DASF 42: Data-centric MLOps and LLMOps promote models as code and automate ML tasks for cross-environment reproducibility
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to track access to data, AI and other resources

• Regulatory non-compliance

risks.title: Model drift
risks.description:
Model drift in machine learning systems can occur due to changes in feature data or target dependencies. This drift can be broadly classified into three scenarios:
Concept drift: where the statistical properties of the target variable change over time

Data drift: involving changes in the distribution of input data

Upstream data changes: occur due to alterations in data collection or processing methods before the data reaches the model

Clever attackers can exploit these scenarios to evade an ML system for adversarial purposes.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 16: Secure model features to track changes to features
• DASF 17: Track training data with MLflow and Delta Lake to track upstream data changes 
• DASF 21: Monitor data and AI system from a single pane of glass for changes and take action when changes occur. Have a feedback loop from a monitoring system and refresh models over time to help avoid model staleness.
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability

risks.title: Lack of Interpretability and Explainability
risks.description:
A lack of interpretability and explainability poses a unique challenge due to the scale and complexity of frontier or GenAI LLMs. The degree to which we can understand the internal workings of a model and trace its decision-making process refers to interpretability. The ability to provide a human-understandable explanation of a model's outputs or decision-making process refers to explainability. Both interpretability and explainability are required to develop trustworthiness in AI systems and are also required to assist with understanding and mitigating security risks such as Prompt Injection, Model Inversion, Misuse, Data Breach, Data Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Security Auditing and Regulatory Compliance.
References: 
Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety -- A Review
Toward Transparent AI: A Survey on Interpreting the Inner Structures of Deep Neural Networks
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 35: Track model performance to evaluate quality
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts
• DASF 42: Data-centric MLOps and LLMOps promote models as code
• DASF 45: Evaluate models to capture performance insights for language models
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability

Additional controls for consideration:
 - Continuous benchmark testing of features throughout the model lifecycle in prediction accuracy, traceability and decision understanding. LIME, SHAP, DEEPLIFT and dashboards of factors influencing decisions.
 - Isolate functionality using a modular architecture. 
 - Implement Explainable AI tools and techniques that can generate human-understandable explanations for model outputs.
 - Model Cards, or a data sheet that provides information on data training sets, known biases, evaluation tests, intended uses, and unintended uses. From the perspective of how the AI Developer trained the model or how my organization has modified the model if my organization has fine-tuned that model.
 - Red Teaming and Adversarial Machine Learning
 - Human in the loop or Human at the helm.

Please see DASF 2.0 section "Resources and Further Reading" for a collection of third-party tools.

risks.title: Backdoor machine learning / Trojaned model
risks.description: There are inherent risks when using public ML/LLM models or outsourcing their training, akin to the dangers associated with executable (.exe) files. A malicious third party handling the training process could tamper with the data or deliver a “Trojan model” that intentionally misclassifies specific inputs. Additionally, open source models may contain hidden malicious code that can exfiltrate sensitive data upon deployment. These risks are pertinent in both external models and outsourced model development scenarios, necessitating scrutiny and verification of models before use.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects 
• DASF 19: Manage end-to-end machine learning lifecycle
• DASF 23: Register, version, approve, promote and deploy models and scan models for malicious code when using third-party models or libraries
• DASF 34: Run models in multiple layers of isolation. Models are considered untrusted code: deploy models and custom LLMs with multiple layers of isolation. 
• DASF 42: Data-centric MLOps and LLMOps promote models as code using CI/CD.
Scan third-party models continuously to identify hidden cybersecurity risks and threats such as malware, vulnerabilities and integrity issues to detect possible signs of malicious activity, including malware, tampering and backdoors. See resources section for third-party tools.
• DASF 43: Use access control lists to limit who can bring models and limit the use of public models
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs
• DASF 56: Restrict outbound connections from models to prevent attacks to exfiltrate data, inference requests and responses
• DASF 67: Federate authentication

Additional controls to consider: 
Please see the companion compendium document for a collection of third-party tools.

risks.title: ML Supply chain vulnerabilities
risks.description: Due to the extensive data, skills and computational resources required to train machine learning algorithms, it’s common practice to reuse and slightly modify models developed by large corporations. For example, ResNet, a popular image recognition model from Microsoft, is often adapted for customer-specific tasks. These models are curated in a Model Zoo (Caffe hosts popular image recognition models) or hosted by third-party ML SaaS (OpenAI LLMs are an example). In this attack, the adversary attacks the models hosted in Caffe, thereby poisoning the well for anyone else. Adversaries can also host specialized models that will receive less scrutiny, akin to watering hole attacks.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 22: Build models with all representative, accurate and relevant data sources to minimize third-party dependencies for models and data where possible
• DASF 27: Pretrain a large language model (LLM) on your own IP
• DASF 42: Data-centric MLOps and LLMOps promote models as code using CI/CD. 
Scan third-party models continuously to identify hidden cybersecurity risks and threats such as malware, vulnerabilities and integrity issues to detect possible signs of malicious activity, including malware, tampering and backdoors. See resources section for third-party tools. 
• DASF 45: Evaluate models and validate (aka, stress testing) to verify reported function and disclosed weaknesses in the models
• DASF 48: Use hardened runtime for machine learning 
• DASF 53: Third-party library control
• DASF 56: Restrict outbound connections from models to prevent attacks to exfiltrate data, inference requests and responses

Additional controls to consider: 
Please see the companion compendium document for a collection of third-party tools.

risks.title: Model theft
risks.description:
Training machine learning systems, particularly large language models, involves considerable investment. A significant risk is the potential theft of a system’s knowledge through direct observation of their input and output observations, akin to reverse engineering. This can lead to unauthorized access, copying or exfiltration of proprietary models, resulting in economic losses, eroded competitive advantage and exposure of sensitive information.
This attack can be as simple as attackers making legitimate queries and analyzing the responses to recreate a model. Once replicated, the model can be inverted, enabling the attackers to extract feature information or infer details about the training data.

risks.description: A direct prompt injection occurs when a user injects text that is intended to alter the behavior of the LLM. Malicious input, known as model evasion in the MITRE ATLAS framework, is a significant threat to machine learning systems. These risks manifest as “adversarial examples”: inputs deliberately designed to deceive models. Attackers use direct prompt injections to bypass safeguards in order to create misinformation and cause reputational damage. Attackers may wish to extract the system prompt or reveal private information provided to the model in the context but not intended for unfiltered access by the user. Large language model (LLM) plug-ins are particularly vulnerable, as they are typically required to handle untrusted input and it is difficult to apply adequate application control. Attackers can exploit such vulnerabilities, with severe potential outcomes including remote code execution.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform
• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to access data
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform 
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources 
• DASF 24: Control access to models and model assets 
• DASF 46: Store and retrieve embeddings securely to integrate data objects for security-sensitive data that goes into LLMs as RAG inputs
• DASF 30: Encrypt models
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints 
• DASF 32: Streamline the usage and management of various large language model (LLM) providers and rate-limit inference queries allowed by the model.
Designing robust prompts can help mitigate attacks such as jailbreaking.
Implement gates between users/callers and the actual model by performing input validation post-processing on all proposed queries, rejecting anything not meeting the model’s definition of input correctness, and returning only the minimum amount of information needed to be useful.

• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts

• DASF 60: Rate limit number of inference queries
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability
• DASF 67: Federate authentication

risks.title: Model breakout
risks.description: Malicious users can exploit adversarial examples to mislead machine learning systems, including large language models (LLMs). These specially crafted inputs aim to disrupt the normal functioning of these systems, leading to several potential hazards. An attacker might use these examples to force the system to deviate from its intended environment, exfiltrate sensitive data or interact inappropriately with other systems. Additionally, adversarial inputs can cause false predictions, leak sensitive information from the training data, or manipulate the system into executing unintended actions on internal and external systems.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 34: Run models in multiple layers of isolation with unprivileged VMs and network segregation. Protects back-end internal systems from LLM access. The most reliable mitigation is to always treat all LLM output as potentially malicious and remember that an untrusted entity has been able to inject text as user input. All LLM output should be inspected and sanitized before being further parsed to extract information related to the plug-in. Plug-in templates should be parameterized wherever possible, and any calls to external services must be strictly parameterized at all times and made in a least-privileged context. 
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts
• DASF 56: Restrict outbound connections from models to prevent attacks to exfiltrate data, inference requests and responses

risks.title: Looped input
risks.description: There is a notable risk in machine learning systems when the output produced by the system is reintroduced into the real world and subsequently cycles back as input, creating a harmful feedback loop. This can reinforce removing security filters, biases or errors, potentially leading to increasingly skewed or inaccurate model performance and unintended system behaviors.
risks.source_control_guidance: • DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging models to capture incoming requests and outgoing responses to your model serving endpoint and automatically log them in tables. Afterward, you can use the data in this table to monitor, debug and improve ML models and decide if these inferences are of sufficient quality for input to model training.

risks.title: Infer training data membership
risks.description:
Adversaries may pose a significant privacy threat to machine learning systems by simulating or inferring whether specific data samples were part of a model’s training set. Such inferences can be made by:
Using techniques like Train Proxy via Replication to create and host shadow models replicating the target model’s behavior

Analyzing the statistical patterns in the model’s prediction scores to conclude the training data


These methods can lead to the unintended leakage of sensitive information, such as individuals’ personally identifiable information (PII) in the training dataset or other forms of protected intellectual property.

risks.title: Accidental exposure of unauthorized data to models
risks.description:
In GenAI, large language models (LLMs)
are also becoming an integral part of the infrastructure and software applications. LLMs are being used to create more powerful online search, help software developers write
code, and even power chatbots that help with customer service. LLMs are being integrated with corporate databases and documents to enable powerful retrieval augmented generation (RAG) scenarios when LLMs are adapted to specific domains and use cases. For example: rows from a database or text from a PDF document that are intended to be summarized generically by the LLM. These scenarios in effect expose a new attack surface to potentially confidential and proprietary enterprise data that is not sufficiently secured or overprivileged, which can lead to use of unauthorized data as an input source to models. A similar risk exists for tabular data models that rely upon lookups to feature store tables at inference time.

• DASF 58: Protect data with filters and masking
• DASF 57: Use attribute-based access controls (ABAC)
• DASF 59: Use clean rooms to collaborate in a secure environment

risks.title: Lack of MLOps — repeatable enforced standards
risks.description:
Operationalizing an ML solution requires joining data from predictions, monitoring and feature tables with other relevant data. 
Duplicating data, moving AI assets, and driving governance and tracking across these stages may represent roadblocks to practitioners who would rather shortcut security controls to deliver their solution. Many organizations will find that the simplest way to securely combine ML solutions, input data and feature tables is to leverage the same platform that manages other production data.
An ML solution comprises data, code and models. These assets must be developed, tested (staging) and deployed (production). For each of these stages, we also need to operate within an execution environment. Security is an essential component of all MLOps lifecycle stages. It ensures the complete lifecycle meets the required standards by keeping the distinct execution environments — development, staging and production.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 42: Data-centric MLOps and LLMOps. MLOps best practices: separate environments by workspace and schema, promote models with code, MLOps Stacks for repeatable ML infra across environments
• DASF 45: Evaluate models to capture performance insights for language models
• DASF 44: Trigger actions in response to a specific event to trigger automated jobs to keep human-in-the-loop (HITL)

risks.title: Lack of penetration testing, red teaming and bug bounty
risks.description:
Penetration testing and bug bounty programs are vital in securing software that supports data and AI/ML operations. Unlike in direct attacks on AI/ML algorithms, adversaries often target underlying software risks, such as the OWASP Top 10. These foundational software layers are generally more prone to attacks than the AI/ML components.  AI red teaming, especially for large language models, is an important component of developing and deploying models safely.

Penetration testing involves skilled experts actively seeking and exploiting weaknesses, mimicking real attack scenarios. Bug bounty programs encourage external ethical hackers to find and report vulnerabilities, rewarding them for their discoveries. This combination of internal and external security testing enhances overall system protection, safeguarding the integrity of AI/ML infrastructures against cyber threats.
risks.source_control_guidance: • DASF 39: Platform Security — Penetration testing and bug bounty to build, deploy and monitor ML/AI models on a platform that takes responsibility seriously and shares remediation timeline commitments. A bug bounty program removes a barrier researchers face in working with Databricks.

risks.title: Memory Poisoning
risks.description: Memory Poisoning involves exploiting an AI's memory systems, both short and long-term, to introduce malicious or false data and exploit the agent’s context. This can lead to altered decision-making and unauthorized operations.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform
• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to access data
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources
• DASF 24: Control access to models and model assets, AI agents
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints
• DASF 34: Run models and agents in multiple layers of isolation with unprivileged VMs and network segregation. Protects back-end internal systems. Implement memory content validation, session isolation, robust authentication mechanisms for memory access, anomaly detection systems, and regular memory sanitization routines.
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts
• DASF 46: Store and retrieve embeddings securely to protect vector store memory — a primary long-term memory store for agents — from unauthorized access and injection
• DASF 54: Implement LLM guardrails to prevent unwanted and unsafe data in requests and responses
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to detect unauthorized reads and writes to agent memory stores
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents, applying least privilege to what agents can read from and write to memory, limiting the blast radius of a poisoning attempt
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability
• DASF 67: Federate authentication
• DASF 71: Log and register AI agents to provide traceability on which agent modified memory, enabling attribution and forensics
• DASF 72: Securely store and reuse agent state to protect short-term agent memory (conversation history, decision logs, temporary tasks) within a governed perimeter rather than insecure external stores

risks.title: Cascading Hallucination Attacks
risks.description: These attacks exploit an AI's tendency to generate contextually plausible but false information, which can propagate through systems and disrupt decision-making. This can also lead to destructive reasoning affecting tools invocation.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints
• DASF 34: Run models in multiple layers of isolation with unprivileged VMs and network segregation to contain the impact of cascading false outputs across systems
• DASF 36: Set up monitoring alerts to automatically detect output divergence patterns and unusual tool invocation sequences indicative of a hallucination cascade in progress
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts and monitor tool usage patterns. Establish robust output validation mechanisms and implement behavioral alerts to detect hallucination propagation
• DASF 39: Platform security — Incident Response Team to coordinate response when a hallucination cascade is detected
• DASF 45: Evaluate models using Mosaic AI Model Evaluation to assess hallucination rates and output reliability pre-deployment. Use LLM-as-a-judge metrics to establish a hallucination baseline before models are used in agentic pipelines
• DASF 49: Automate LLM evaluation to evaluate RAG applications with LLM-as-a-judge and get out-of-the-box metrics like toxicity, latency, tokens and more. Quickly and efficiently compare and contrast various LLMs to navigate your RAG application requirements
• DASF 54: Implement AI guardrails to filter and block hallucinated or unsafe outputs at the serving layer before they can propagate downstream
• DASF 60: Rate limit number of inference queries. Implement AI rate-limiting policies to restrict high-frequency task requests per agent session, which can help throttle cascading effects in multi-agent pipelines before they compound
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability to record the chain of reasoning and tool invocations that led to a hallucinated output, enabling root-cause analysis
• DASF 66: Use Human-in-the-loop feedback to deploy multi-source validation and ensure ongoing system corrections through feedback loops. Require secondary validation of AI-generated knowledge before it is used in critical decision-making processes

risks.title: Intent Breaking & Goal Manipulation
risks.description: This threat exploits vulnerabilities in an AI agent's planning and goal-setting capabilities, allowing attackers to manipulate or redirect the agent's objectives and reasoning. One common approach is Agent Hijacking, where an AI agent ingests adversarial manipulated data and subsequently executes unintended actions aligned with the attacker's goals rather than the user's intent.

• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to access data
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources
• DASF 24: Control access to models and model assets, AI agents, to enforce strict tool access verification

  memory access, anomaly detection systems, and regular memory sanitization routines.
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts and monitor tool usage patterns for signs of goal deviation
• DASF 49: Automate LLM evaluation to identify quality issues and determine the root cause of those issues by having another model check the agent and flag significant goal deviations that could indicate manipulation
• DASF 54: Implement LLM guardrails to prevent unwanted and unsafe data in requests and responses, validate agent instructions, and set clear operational boundaries to detect and prevent misuse
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to detect when agent reasoning and actions deviate significantly from its declared objectives, flagging potential goal manipulation
• DASF 56: Restrict outbound connections from models to prevent a goal-manipulated agent from making unauthorized external calls or exfiltrating data in service of the attacker's redirected objective
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents, applying least privilege so that even a successfully manipulated agent is constrained in what actions it can execute
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability to record reasoning chains and detect where goal manipulation was introduced, enabling post-incident forensics
• DASF 66: Use Human-in-the-loop feedback to require human approval before the agent takes high-stakes or irreversible actions, providing an effective checkpoint against goal-redirected behavior
• DASF 67: Federate authentication
• DASF 71: Log and register AI agents to maintain a known baseline of each agent's intended goals, making deviations detectable
• DASF 73: Register prompts using MLflow prompt registry to version and govern system prompts. A well-designed, hardened system prompt that clearly encodes the agent's goals is a direct defense against intent-breaking and goal  manipulation attacks

risks.title: Overwhelming Human in the Loop
risks.description: This threat targets systems with human oversight and decision validation, aiming to exploit human cognitive limitations or compromise interaction frameworks. Attackers may flood agents with decision requests to cause approval fatigue, or embed malicious actions within a high volume of legitimate requests to bypass human scrutiny.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 36: Set up monitoring alerts to detect unusual volumes of human approval requests and alert when request rates indicate a request-flooding or overwhelming pattern
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables to monitor human decision approval patterns over time and identify anomalies such as unusual frequency or clustering of high-risk decisions
• DASF 49: Automate LLM evaluation to evaluate agent behavior and use built-in AI judges to pre-filter low-risk decisions, reducing the volume of requests that reach human reviewers
• DASF 60: Rate limit number of inference queries to prevent request flooding that can overwhelm human reviewers. Restrict high-frequency task requests per agent session on a per-user and per-endpoint basis.
• DASF 66: Use Human-in-the-loop feedback to deploy multi-source validation and ensure ongoing system corrections through feedback loops. Design HITL checkpoints to be targeted to genuinely high-risk decisions rather than exhaustively reviewing every agent action.

  Develop advanced human-AI interaction frameworks and adaptive trust mechanisms. These are dynamic AI governance models that employ dynamic intervention thresholds to adjust the level of human oversight and automation based on risk, confidence, and context.

risks.title: Unexpected RCE and Code Attacks
risks.description: Attackers exploit AI-generated execution environments to inject malicious code, trigger unintended system behaviors, or execute unauthorized scripts.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 34: Run models in multiple layers of isolation with unprivileged VMs and network segregation. Protects back-end internal systems from LLM access. The most reliable mitigation is to always treat all LLM and agent output as potentially malicious — an untrusted entity has been able to inject text as user input. Restrict AI code generation permissions, sandbox execution environments, and monitor AI-generated scripts before and during execution.
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty, and vulnerability management. Conduct regular sandbox breakout testing to validate that AI code execution environments are properly hardened and that RCE vulnerabilities cannot be chained to escape the execution boundary.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to detect unusual code execution patterns, unauthorized script launches, and anomalous system calls that may indicate successful or attempted RCE
• DASF 56: Restrict outbound connections from models to prevent AI-generated code — if executed — from phoning home, establishing reverse shells, or exfiltrating data to attacker-controlled endpoints
• DASF 62: Implement network segmentation to isolate AI code execution environments from sensitive internal systems, limiting the lateral movement capability of any successfully executed malicious code
• DASF 63: Update software to patch AI code execution environments, sandboxes, and container runtimes. Unpatched execution environments provide footholds for privilege escalation and sandbox escape.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents, applying least privilege to execution environments so that even successfully executed malicious code has constrained access to system resources and data
• DASF 71: Log and register AI agents to maintain traceability of which agent generated and executed code, enabling attribution and forensic analysis following an RCE incident

• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty, and vulnerability management. Conduct red team exercises specifically targeting multi-agent trust boundaries and rogue agent scenarios to identify weaknesses before attackers do.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs for continuous behavioral monitoring of all agent activity, detecting agents operating outside normal boundaries, taking unauthorized actions, or exhibiting patterns inconsistent with their registered purpose

• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents, applying policy constraints so that even a rogue agent is restricted to only what it was explicitly authorized to access — minimizing the damage it can cause

risks.description: In scenarios where AI agents engage in direct interaction with human users, the trust relationship reduces user skepticism, increasing reliance on the agent's responses and autonomy. This implicit trust and direct human/agent interaction create risks, as attackers can coerce agents to manipulate users, spread misinformation, and take covert actions.

• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts. Monitor inputs and outputs for deviations that may indicate an agent is being coerced into producing manipulative or misleading content for users
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty, and vulnerability management. Include user-manipulation and social engineering scenarios in red team exercises targeting agent-user interaction surfaces.
• DASF 54: Implement AI guardrails to detect and block manipulative, misleading, and harmful content in agent responses before they reach users. Guardrails are the most direct technical control for preventing agents from spreading
   misinformation or executing covert manipulative actions.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to implement comprehensive logging of all user-facing agent interactions, enabling detection of patterns indicative of manipulation campaigns or covert influence operations

risks.title: Prompt Injection
risks.description: Prompt injection attacks occur when malicious prompts manipulate MCP server behavior or bypass security controls. This includes direct injection through user input, indirect injection through data sources, and manipulation of tool descriptions. These attacks can lead to unauthorized actions, data exfiltration, and privilege escalation, making this the most critical MCP security risk.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources
• DASF 24: Control access to models and model assets, AI agents
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints
• DASF 32: Streamline the usage and management of various large language model (LLM) providers and rate-limit inference queries. Design robust prompts to help mitigate injection attacks. Implement gates between users/callers and
  the actual model by performing input validation and post-processing on all proposed queries, rejecting anything not meeting the model's definition of input correctness, and returning only the minimum amount of information needed.
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging prompts. Monitor for injection patterns in inputs and flag suspicious prompt structures
• DASF 46: Store and retrieve embeddings securely to protect vector store data sources from indirect prompt injection via poisoned retrieval content
• DASF 54: Implement AI guardrails to detect and block prompt injection attempts, filter malicious inputs, and prevent unsafe outputs triggered by injected instructions
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to detect prompt injection patterns, flag anomalous MCP server behavior, and identify sequences indicative of successful injection and privilege escalation
• DASF 56: Restrict outbound connections from models to prevent successful prompt injections from exfiltrating data or establishing unauthorized external connections
• DASF 60: Rate limit number of inference queries to throttle injection attempts that rely on high-volume probing
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents, applying least privilege so that even a successfully injected prompt has constrained scope for unauthorized actions
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability to record all MCP server inputs and tool invocations, enabling forensic analysis following an injection incident
• DASF 67: Federate authentication to ensure all MCP server interactions are tied to verified identities
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers. Databricks-managed MCP servers are hosted within the security boundary of your workspace, reducing the attack surface for prompt injection via external MCP channels
• DASF 73: Register prompts using MLflow prompt registry to govern and version system prompts. Well-designed system prompts with explicit injection-resistance instructions reduce susceptibility to direct and indirect prompt
  injection attacks.

risks.title: Confused Deputy
risks.description: The confused deputy problem occurs when MCP servers perform actions on behalf of the wrong user or with incorrect permissions. This can result in authorization bypass, cross-user data access, and privilege escalation. The complexity of MCP's role-based interactions makes this vulnerability particularly dangerous in multi-user environments.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform and establish a strong identity foundation for all MCP interactions
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists to limit the sources that can authenticate to your data and AI platform
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources
• DASF 24: Control access to models and model assets, AI agents, to enforce strict access verification and prevent unauthorized permission delegation
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty, and vulnerability management. Include confused deputy and MCP delegation scenarios in security testing.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs to detect when MCP server actions are being performed under an incorrect user identity or with permissions that don't match the requesting principal
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents. The on-behalf-of-user authentication feature is the primary Databricks control for the confused deputy problem — agents access Databricks resources using the identity of the end user who queried the agent, ensuring fine-grained, per-user access control rather than broad agent-level permissions.
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability to maintain a full audit trail of which user triggered which agent action, enabling identification and attribution of confused deputy incidents
• DASF 67: Federate authentication using OAuth token federation to maintain proper user identity throughout agent delegation chains, preventing identity loss or substitution during MCP interactions
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers. Databricks-managed MCP servers are built with proper OAuth-based authentication that ties MCP actions to the requesting user's identity, directly mitigating the confused deputy problem.
• DASF 71: Log and register AI agents to maintain an authoritative record of which agents are authorized to act on behalf of which users, making unauthorized delegation detectable

risks.title: Tool Poisoning
risks.description: Tool poisoning involves malicious tools masquerading as legitimate ones, or legitimate tools with malicious descriptions designed to trick AI models. Examples include fake tool descriptions, malicious tool implementations, and tool name squatting. This attack vector exploits the trust relationship between AI models and their available tools.

• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources
• DASF 24: Control access to models and model assets, AI agents, to enforce strict tool access verification and restrict which tools agents are permitted to invoke
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints
• DASF 32: Streamline the usage and management of various LLM providers. Design robust prompts to help mitigate tool manipulation attacks. Implement gates between users and models by performing input validation on all proposed tool calls.
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables to monitor tool call patterns. Detect when tools behave unexpectedly relative to their declared descriptions, which may indicate a poisoned or substituted tool.
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty, and vulnerability management. Include tool poisoning scenarios (fake tool descriptions, name squatting, tool substitution) in red team exercises to validate tool supply chain integrity.
• DASF 46: Store and retrieve embeddings securely to protect vector store data that agents use to discover and select tools from potential tool description poisoning
• DASF 54: Implement AI guardrails to validate tool calls and detect when tool descriptions or tool responses contain suspicious or malicious instructions

risks.title: Credential and Token Exposure
risks.description: Credential and token exposure occurs through improper handling, storage, or transmission of API keys, OAuth tokens, and other sensitive credentials. This includes hardcoded credentials, token theft, and credential leakage in logs. Given MCP's reliance on API integrations, credential security is fundamental to overall system security.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 8: Encrypt data at rest — Store MCP server credentials, API keys, and tokens using Databricks customer-managed encryption keys to protect sensitive authentication material at rest.
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — Ensure tokens and credentials transmitted between MCP servers, clients, and external services are encrypted using TLS 1.2+ to prevent interception during transit.
• DASF 33: Manage credentials securely — Use Databricks Secrets to store API keys, OAuth tokens, and service credentials referenced by MCP servers. Never hardcode credentials in MCP server code, configuration files, or agent prompts. Reference secrets programmatically rather than passing them as plaintext.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — Monitor audit logs and system tables for unusual authentication events, failed credential attempts, and unexpected API access patterns that may indicate credential theft or token misuse.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — Apply least privilege to MCP server credentials. Each agent should only receive the minimum set of credentials necessary to perform its authorized functions, reducing the blast  radius if credentials are compromised.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — Use OAuth token federation to authenticate to Databricks and external services, eliminating the need for static API keys or hardcoded service principal credentials in MCP server configurations. Token federation reduces the risk of long-lived credential theft.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers — Databricks managed MCP servers handle credential management securely, removing the burden of manual secret rotation and reducing credential exposure risk inherent in custom MCP configurations.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers — Deploy custom or third-party MCP servers as Databricks Apps to leverage built-in secure secret management. Databricks Apps prevent credentials from being exposed in environment variables or configuration files accessible to unauthorized parties.
• DASF 71: Log and register AI agents — Register all AI agents that access MCP credentials in the Databricks AI Agent Framework. Maintain a registry of which agents have access to which credentials, enabling rapid audit and revocation in the event of a credential compromise.

risks.title: Supply Chain Attacks

risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty and vulnerability management — conduct regular security assessments of MCP server integrations and third-party dependencies to identify supply chain vulnerabilities before they are exploited.
• DASF 53: Third-party library control — manage and govern the installation and usage of third-party MCP servers and their dependencies. Validate the provenance and integrity of all external MCP components. Avoid using unverified or community-maintained MCP servers without proper vetting.

• DASF 63: Update software — patch and update MCP server software and dependencies regularly to address known vulnerabilities. Monitor for abandoned or deprecated MCP server projects and proactively migrate away from unmaintained dependencies.

• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — use Databricks managed MCP proxies and Unity Catalog HTTP connections to securely authenticate to external MCP servers. Validate the identity and integrity of external servers before granting agent access.

risks.title: Excessive Permissions and Scope Creep
risks.description: Excessive permissions occur when MCP servers request more permissions than necessary for their intended function, or when privileges gradually escalate over time. This includes overprivileged OAuth scopes, unnecessary file system access, and excessive API permissions that increase the potential impact of a compromise.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects — implement a permissions model across all data assets accessed by MCP servers. Regularly review and prune permissions to prevent accumulation of unnecessary access over time.
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty and vulnerability management — conduct regular reviews of MCP server permission scopes to identify overprivileged configurations and scope creep.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — track permission usage over time to detect scope creep. Alert on MCP servers or agents accessing resources beyond their originally granted scopes.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — enforce least privilege for all MCP servers and agents. Each server should only be granted the minimum OAuth scopes, file system access, and API permissions needed for its specific function.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — use OAuth token federation with precisely scoped tokens. Define narrow, task-specific OAuth scopes for each MCP server integration to prevent overprivileged access.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers — Databricks managed MCP servers use OAuth and PAT authentication with controlled permission scopes, reducing the risk of overprivileged server configurations.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps with OAuth authentication and explicitly defined permission boundaries, preventing scope creep in custom deployments.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — validate the permission scopes requested by external MCP servers before granting access. Reject connections from servers requesting broader permissions than their stated  function requires.

risks.title: Data Exfiltration
risks.description: Data exfiltration involves unauthorized access to or transmission of sensitive data through MCP channels. This can occur through sensitive data in responses, covert channels, or unauthorized data access. The ability of MCP servers to access diverse data sources makes this a significant concern for data protection.
risks.source_control_guidance:
Deploy Agents and MCP servers (managed and custom) with secure defaults and require clients to specify authentication.
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform.
• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to access data.
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform.
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests.
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources.
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — ensure all data transmitted through MCP channels is encrypted to prevent interception.
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints — prevent unauthorized access to MCP endpoints that could be used as exfiltration channels.
• DASF 33: Manage credentials securely — prevent credentials of data sources from leaking through MCP server responses.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect unusual data access and transmission patterns indicative of exfiltration. Alert on large data transfers, unexpected resource access, or responses containing sensitive data patterns.
• DASF 56: Restrict outbound connections from models — limit the external destinations that MCP servers can transmit data to. Block unauthorized outbound connections that could serve as covert exfiltration channels.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — enforce least privilege so agents and MCP servers can only access the minimum data needed, reducing the volume of data that could be exfiltrated.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — use OAuth token federation to control and audit which data sources MCP servers can access, preventing unauthorized data retrieval.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers — Databricks managed MCP servers enforce data access controls and prevent unauthorized data transmission through governed MCP channels.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps with controlled data access and egress policies.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — validate external MCP server destinations before establishing connections to prevent data being transmitted to unauthorized endpoints.

risks.title: Context Spoofing and Manipulation
risks.description: Context spoofing involves manipulation of context information provided to AI models to alter their behavior in unintended ways. Attacks target flaws in protocols like MCP or A2A, such as consent bypass or context hijacking, leading to unauthorized agent actions. This includes fake context injection, context poisoning, and state manipulation. These attacks exploit the AI model’s reliance on context to make decisions about tool usage.
risks.source_control_guidance:
Deploy Agents and MCP servers (managed and custom) with secure defaults and require clients to specify authentication.
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform.
• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to access data.
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform.
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests.
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources.
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — protect context data transmitted between MCP components from interception and tampering.
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints — prevent unauthorized parties from injecting manipulated context through exposed endpoints.
• DASF 33: Manage credentials securely — prevent credential-based context spoofing where attackers use stolen credentials to inject false identity context.
• DASF 37: Set up inference tables for monitoring and debugging — capture and analyze context inputs and outputs to detect spoofed or manipulated context patterns. Flag deviations from expected context structures.
• DASF 54: Implement AI guardrails — validate context integrity before it is processed by the agent. Reject context that contains injection patterns, unexpected state changes, or inconsistencies with the established session.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect anomalous context patterns such as unexpected consent bypass attempts, state manipulation, or context inconsistencies that indicate spoofing.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — enforce least privilege so that even successfully spoofed context cannot grant access beyond the agent's authorized scope.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — enforce strong agent-to-agent authentication to prevent context spoofing through identity impersonation in multi-agent workflows.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers — enforce strong agent-to-agent authentication on managed MCP servers, ensuring context integrity across agent communications.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers — enforce strong agent-to-agent authentication on custom MCP servers to prevent context hijacking in custom deployments.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — enforce strong agent-to-agent authentication when connecting to external MCP servers to prevent context spoofing from untrusted sources.

risks.title: Insecure Communication
risks.description: Insecure communication encompasses unencrypted or improperly secured communication channels between MCP components. This includes unencrypted transport, weak TLS implementation, and vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks. Secure communication is fundamental to preventing interception of sensitive data and credentials.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists — limit the sources permitted to initiate communication with MCP servers, reducing the attack surface for man-in-the-middle interception.
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link — enforce private network paths for MCP communication to prevent traffic from traversing untrusted public networks where interception is possible.
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — enforce TLS 1.2+ for all communication between MCP clients, servers, and external endpoints. Reject weak cipher suites and prevent protocol downgrade attacks.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect communication anomalies such as failed TLS handshakes, unexpected connection attempts, and indicators of man-in-the-middle activity.
• DASF 62: Implement network segmentation — isolate MCP communication channels from general network traffic to limit exposure and contain the impact of any communication compromise.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers — Databricks managed MCP servers enforce TLS encryption by default, eliminating the risk of misconfigured or absent encryption in self-managed deployments.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps, which enforces secure communication standards and prevents weak TLS configurations in custom implementations.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — use Databricks managed MCP proxies to enforce secure, encrypted connections to external MCP servers. Validate TLS certificates and reject connections from servers with invalid or untrusted certificates.

risks.title: Malicious Server Connection
risks.description: Malicious server connection occurs when clients connect to compromised or malicious MCP servers without proper validation. This includes fake servers, DNS poisoning, server impersonation, and connection hijacking. The distributed nature of MCP server deployment makes it easy for attackers to create malicious servers that appear legitimate to unsuspecting clients.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — enforce TLS certificate validation when connecting to MCP servers. Reject connections from servers with invalid, expired, or untrusted certificates that may indicate server impersonation or DNS poisoning.
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty and vulnerability management — regularly test MCP client configurations for susceptibility to malicious server connections and server impersonation attacks.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect connections to unexpected or unauthorized MCP servers. Alert on new server connections, DNS resolution anomalies, and certificate changes that may indicate connection hijacking.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers with OAuth and PAT authentication — connect to Databricks managed MCP servers as trusted, verified endpoints, reducing reliance on externally hosted servers that may be  compromised.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers with OAuth authentication — host custom MCP servers within Databricks to ensure client connections remain within a trusted, governed environment. 
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — use Databricks managed MCP proxies and Unity Catalog HTTP connections to authenticate external server connections. Only connect to known, pre-approved MCP servers using OAuth to prevent connection to malicious imposters.

risks.title: Insecure Credential Storage
risks.description: Insecure credential storage involves improper storage of MCP server credentials, API keys, and authentication tokens on the client system. This includes plaintext credentials, weak encryption, accessible credential files, and inadequate protection of sensitive authentication data. Client-side credential storage is particularly vulnerable to local attacks and system compromise.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 8: Encrypt data at rest — ensure all MCP client credentials, API keys, and authentication tokens stored on the client system are encrypted at rest. Never store credentials in plaintext configuration files or accessible credential stores.
• DASF 33: Manage credentials securely — use Databricks Secrets to store MCP server credentials and authentication tokens rather than plaintext files or environment variables. Reference secrets programmatically to prevent exposure in code or configuration.
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty and vulnerability management — test MCP client systems for insecure credential storage vulnerabilities, including accessible credential files, weak encryption, and inadequate access controls on secret stores.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect unauthorized access to client credential stores and alert on unusual credential retrieval patterns that may indicate local compromise or credential theft.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — use OAuth token federation to authenticate to MCP servers, eliminating the need for long-lived static credentials stored on the client. Short-lived federated tokens reduce the risk from client-side credential compromise.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers with OAuth and PAT authentication — authenticate to managed MCP servers using OAuth, avoiding the need to store static API keys or service credentials on the client.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers with OAuth authentication — authenticate to custom MCP servers using OAuth to minimize the use of long-lived credentials that require secure client-side storage.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — use Databricks managed MCP proxies to handle authentication to external servers, centralizing credential management and removing the need for clients to store external server credentials locally.

risks.title: UI/UX Deception
risks.description: UI/UX deception involves misleading users about MCP server actions, permissions, or capabilities through the client interface. This includes hidden tool calls, misleading permission dialogs, unclear action descriptions, and interfaces that don't clearly communicate what actions are being performed. Users may unknowingly authorize dangerous operations
risks.source_control_guidance:
Deploy Agents and MCP servers (managed and custom) with secure defaults and require clients to specify authentication.
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access your data and AI platform.
• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to access data.
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform.
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests.
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources.
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — protect communications between client and MCP servers from interception and tampering.
• DASF 31: Secure model serving endpoints — prevent unauthorized exposure of endpoints that could be exploited to deliver deceptive UI content.
• DASF 33: Manage credentials securely — prevent credentials from being harvested through deceptive permission dialogs or fake authentication prompts.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect discrepancies between actions presented to users and actions actually executed by MCP clients. Alert on hidden tool calls or actions that were not clearly communicated in the interface.
• DASF 61: Train users on AI/ML security — educate users to recognize deceptive UI patterns such as misleading permission dialogs, hidden tool calls, and unclear action descriptions. Establish organizational guidance on what legitimate MCP permission requests look like.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — enforce least privilege so that even if a user is deceived into authorizing an action, the agent cannot access resources beyond its permitted scope.
• DASF 65: Implement end-to-end AI traceability — make all agent actions and tool calls visible and auditable, enabling users to verify that the actions taken match what was displayed in the interface.

• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps with verified, transparent interfaces that accurately represent the actions and permissions they require.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — validate external MCP server interfaces before use. Reject connections to servers presenting misleading or non-standard permission requests.

risks.title: Insufficient Server Validation
risks.description: Insufficient server validation occurs when clients fail to properly validate MCP server authenticity and integrity before establishing connections. This includes no certificate validation, missing server verification, weak trust models, and inadequate verification of server identity. Without proper validation, clients may connect to malicious servers.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — enforce strict TLS certificate validation for all MCP server connections. Reject servers with invalid, expired, self-signed, or untrusted certificates. Prevent protocol downgrade attacks that   bypass certificate validation.
• DASF 38: Platform security — penetration testing, red teaming, bug bounty and vulnerability management — test MCP client configurations for certificate validation bypasses, weak trust models, and susceptibility to server  impersonation attacks.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect certificate validation failures, unexpected server identity changes, and anomalous connection attempts that indicate insufficient validation is being bypassed or exploited.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — use OAuth token federation as an additional layer of server identity verification. OAuth-based authentication requires servers to present valid credentials from trusted identity providers, supplementing certificate-based validation.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers with OAuth and PAT authentication — Databricks managed MCP servers present verified, trusted identities, eliminating client-side validation uncertainty for managed server connections.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers with OAuth authentication — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps with verified identities, ensuring clients can reliably validate server authenticity before connecting.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — use Databricks managed MCP proxies to handle server identity validation for external connections. Only connect to pre-approved, known MCP servers using OAuth to ensure server authenticity is verified before granting agent access.

risks.title: Client-Side Data Leakage
risks.description: Client-side data leakage involves sensitive data leaking through client logs, caches, temporary files, or local storage mechanisms. This includes credentials in logs, cached sensitive responses, temporary file exposure, and inadequate cleanup of sensitive data. Client systems often store more data than users realize, creating multiple leakage vectors.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA to limit who can access the client system and its locally stored data.
• DASF 2: Sync users and groups to inherit your organizational roles to access data, ensuring only authorized users can access client-side cached data and logs.
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform, limiting exposure of client systems to trusted network sources.
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests, preventing unauthorized access to client systems that may hold cached sensitive data.
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects — restrict access to client-side log files, caches, and temporary storage that may contain sensitive MCP response data.
• DASF 8: Encrypt data at rest — encrypt local client caches, temporary files, and log storage to prevent sensitive data exposure in the event of client system compromise or unauthorized access.
• DASF 33: Manage credentials securely — configure MCP clients to never log credentials, API keys, or authentication tokens. Use Databricks Secrets to ensure sensitive authentication data is not written to local storage or log files.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect unusual access to client-side data stores, log files, and caches that may indicate data exfiltration from local leakage vectors.
• DASF 61: Train users on AI/ML security — educate users about client-side data leakage risks, including the presence of sensitive data in MCP client logs, caches, and temp files. Establish data hygiene practices for clearing sensitive local data.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — restrict the scope of data that MCP clients can retrieve and cache locally, reducing the volume and sensitivity of data exposed through client-side leakage vectors.

risks.title: Excessive Permission Granting
risks.description: Excessive permission granting occurs when clients grant more permissions to MCP servers than necessary for their intended function. This includes overprivileged server access, permission escalation, unnecessary scopes, and inadequate permission review processes. Users may grant broad permissions without understanding the implications.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects — implement a permissions model that enforces granular, task-specific access grants to MCP servers. Establish a permission review process to regularly audit and revoke unnecessary grants.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — track permission grants over time to detect accumulation of unnecessary access. Alert when clients grant permissions beyond established baselines or when permission scopes expand without review.
• DASF 61: Train users on AI/ML security — educate users on the implications of granting broad permissions to MCP servers. Establish organizational guidance on what constitutes acceptable permission scopes and require explicit justification for elevated grants.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — enforce least privilege principles for all MCP server permission grants. Clients should only authorize the minimum permissions required for the specific task, not blanket access to all available resources.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — use OAuth token federation with precisely defined scopes when granting MCP server access. Narrowly scoped OAuth tokens prevent clients from inadvertently granting broader access than intended.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers with OAuth and PAT authentication — Databricks managed MCP servers use controlled permission scopes, reducing the risk of overprivileged grants in managed server interactions.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers with OAuth authentication — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps with explicitly defined permission boundaries, preventing clients from granting excessive access to custom deployments.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — validate and restrict the permission scopes requested by external MCP servers before granting access. Reject connections from external servers requesting broader permissions than their stated function requires.

risks.title: Client-Side Code Execution
risks.description: Client-side code execution involves malicious responses from MCP servers that execute code on the client system. This includes script injection, code execution via responses, client-side attacks through crafted responses, and exploitation of client-side interpreters. Clients that process server responses unsafely are vulnerable to code execution attacks.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 34: Run models in multiple layers of isolation — execute MCP client code and process server responses in sandboxed, isolated environments with unprivileged VMs and network segregation. Treat all MCP server responses as potentially malicious and restrict the ability of response-derived code to interact with the broader system.
• DASF 54: Implement AI guardrails — validate and sanitize all MCP server responses before processing. Detect and block responses containing script injection patterns, embedded executables, or content designed to exploit client-side interpreters.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect anomalous code execution activity on client systems, including unexpected process spawning, unusual file system writes, and network connections initiated by MCP client processes.
• DASF 62: Implement network segmentation — isolate MCP client environments from sensitive internal systems. Contain the impact of successful client-side code execution by preventing compromised clients from traversing to critical infrastructure.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers with OAuth and PAT authentication — Databricks managed MCP servers are vetted and maintained, significantly reducing the risk of malicious responses designed to execute code on client systems.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers with OAuth authentication — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps under organizational control, ensuring server responses are governed and cannot deliver malicious payloads to clients.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — use Databricks managed MCP proxies to intermediate connections to external servers. Only connect to pre-approved external servers, reducing exposure to servers that may deliver malicious response payloads.

risks.title: Session and State Management Failures
risks.description: Session and state management failures involve inadequate management of client sessions, authentication state, and application state. This includes session hijacking, state manipulation, authentication bypass, and inadequate session termination. Poor session management can lead to unauthorized access and privilege escalation.
risks.source_control_guidance:
• DASF 1: SSO with IdP and MFA — enforce strong authentication at session initiation to prevent unauthorized session establishment and authentication bypass.
• DASF 3: Restrict access using IP access lists that can authenticate to your data and AI platform, limiting the network sources from which sessions can be established.
• DASF 4: Restrict access using private link as strong controls that limit the source for inbound requests, ensuring MCP sessions are established only from trusted network paths.
• DASF 5: Control access to data and other objects for permissions model across all data assets to protect data and sources, ensuring session state cannot be manipulated to escalate privileges.
• DASF 9: Encrypt data in transit — protect session tokens and state data transmitted between MCP clients and servers from interception and session hijacking attacks.
• DASF 55: Monitor audit logs — detect session anomalies including simultaneous sessions from different locations, unexpected session state changes, abnormal session durations, and failed authentication attempts that may indicate hijacking or bypass attacks.
• DASF 64: Limit access from AI models and agents — enforce least privilege within sessions so that even a hijacked or manipulated session cannot access resources beyond the agent's authorized scope.
• DASF 67: Federate authentication — use OAuth token federation with short-lived tokens and proper session lifecycle management. Short-lived tokens reduce the window of opportunity for session hijacking and ensure proper session termination.
• DASF 68: Use Securely Hosted Managed MCP Servers with OAuth and PAT authentication — Databricks managed MCP servers implement secure session management by default, reducing client-side session handling complexity.
• DASF 69: Securely host Custom MCP Servers with OAuth authentication — deploy custom MCP servers as Databricks Apps with enforced secure session management, ensuring server-side state is properly protected.
• DASF 70: Securely connect to External MCP Servers — use secure OAuth connections when connecting to external MCP servers to ensure session establishment is properly authenticated and state is securely managed.
• DASF 72: Securely store and reuse agent state — use the Databricks AI Agent Framework to securely store, manage, and restore agent state between sessions. Prevent state tampering by storing agent state in governed, access-controlled storage rather than client-side mechanisms susceptible to manipulation.
